result:
I would give every person an unshakable capacity for empathy—the reflex to see the world through another’s eyes before acting or judging.

Why that, and not an economic, technological, or political reform?

1. Root-cause leverage  
   • Poverty, discrimination, war, and environmental neglect all endure partly because we don’t feel—or choose to ignore—how our choices affect people we’ll never meet.  
   • If empathy were as automatic as sight or hearing, many downstream injustices would be harder to rationalize and easier to solve.

2. Self-correcting power  
   • Empathy compels us to listen, so technocratic or legislative fixes would be refined continually instead of imposed and forgotten.  
   • It would pressure institutions to remain humane as circumstances change.

3. Scalability without coercion  
   • Laws can be broken and resources exhausted, but an internalized moral radar travels with every individual into homes, workplaces, voting booths, and boardrooms.  
   • Unlike a single policy, it wouldn’t hinge on one government or generation.

4. Mental-health dividends  
   • Feeling understood is a protective factor against loneliness, depression, and radicalization.  
   • Empathic people also treat themselves more kindly, reducing cycles of harm.

What might the world look like?

• Diplomacy first: Negotiations replace brinkmanship because leaders intuit the civilian cost of conflict.  
• Inclusive economies: Business models account for worker welfare and environmental impact, shrinking extreme inequality.  
• Smarter climate action: Future generations’ interests feel present, making carbon pricing, conservation, and innovation politically palatable.  
• Nuanced discourse: Online and offline conversations shed some tribalism; disagreement remains, but dehumanization fades.  
• Everyday kindness: Bullying, road rage, and casual cruelty lose their social currency.

Empathy alone won’t plant trees, code vaccines, or rewrite constitutions, but it changes the default setting from “me versus you” to “we live together,” making all those tasks more likely to succeed—and to keep succeeding.
